oneLiner: Cells obey thermodynamics: ΔG (= ΔH − TΔS) sets reaction direction, actual ΔG depends on concentrations, and ATP couples favorable to unfavorable reactions mainly through group transfer.

sections.heading: Metabolism: catabolism vs anabolism
points: Metabolism = sum of all enzyme-catalyzed chemical transformations, organized as ordered metabolic pathways (linear, branched or cyclic).
Catabolism breaks down nutrients, releases energy; generally convergent (many inputs → few common products).
Anabolism builds molecules using energy; generally divergent (few precursors → many products); many anabolic reactions are endergonic.
Opposing pathways use separate enzyme sets, are reciprocally regulated, may use different reaction sequences and different compartments → prevents futile cycling.
Nitrogen needed for amino acids and nucleic acids; energy conversion always loses some free energy as heat (entropy increases).

sections.heading: Enzyme kinetics and regulation
points: Michaelis–Menten: rate rises with [S] and plateaus at Vmax as enzyme saturates (Vmax is for a given enzyme concentration).
Km = substrate concentration at which rate = Vmax/2.
Three regulation modes: substrate availability ([S] low relative to Km limits rate), allosteric regulation (binding away from active site), hormonal regulation (changes enzyme synthesis/degradation).

sections.heading: Thermodynamics: ΔG, ΔH, ΔS
points: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; −ΔH (heat release) and +ΔS (more disorder) both push ΔG negative.
ΔG < 0: exergonic, spontaneous, can do work (many catabolic reactions); ΔG > 0: endergonic, needs input; reverse of endergonic is exergonic.
ΔG < 0 favors forward, > 0 favors reverse, = 0 at equilibrium; spontaneous ≠ fast.
ΔG is a state function: path-independent and additive across sequential reactions.

sections.heading: Standard state, K′eq and actual ΔG
points: Keq = [C]^c[D]^d/[A]^a[B]^b; biochemical standard state: pH 7 ([H⁺] = 10⁻⁷ M), water = 55.5 M, solutes 1 M.
ΔG°′ = −RT ln K′eq: K′eq > 1 → ΔG°′ < 0; K′eq = 1 → 0; K′eq < 1 → ΔG°′ > 0.
Worked example: A ⇌ B, K′eq = 12 → ΔG°′ ≈ −6.15 kJ/mol (favors B).
Actual ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln([products]/[reactants]); concentrations can reverse the favored direction in the cell.
1 kcal = 4.184 kJ.

sections.heading: Reaction coupling
points: Sequential reactions A→B, B→C: shared intermediate cancels; ΔG°′(A→C) = ΔG°′1 + ΔG°′2.
Glucose + Pi → glucose 6-phosphate (+13.8 kJ/mol) coupled with ATP hydrolysis (−30.5) gives net −16.7 kJ/mol.
Glycolysis: glucose → pyruvate; ATP invested in early phosphorylation steps, ATP (substrate-level phosphorylation) and NADH produced later.

sections.heading: ATP as energy currency
points: ATP = adenine + ribose + 3 phosphates; ATP → ADP + Pi or ATP → AMP + PPi, both release energy.
ΔG°′ of ATP hydrolysis = −30.5 kJ/mol; cellular ΔG differs since [ATP], [ADP], [Pi] are unequal and ≪ 1 M (erythrocyte ≈ −51.82 kJ/mol).
Mg²⁺ binds ATP/ADP in cytosol; MgATP²⁻ is the true substrate for most phosphoryl transfers.
ATP/ADP ratio = energy charge signal; low ATP/ADP promotes ATP synthesis by oxidative phosphorylation.
Cells are isothermal: photosynthetic cells capture sunlight, heterotrophs oxidize nutrients; both store energy as ATP.
Redox potential = tendency to donate/accept electrons; depends on reduced:oxidized ratio; NAD⁺/NADH key pair.

sections.heading: High-energy compounds and phosphoryl-transfer potential
points: High-energy compound: releases > 7.0 kcal/mol on hydrolysis (slide's cutoff); many but not all are phosphates.
Classes: acyl phosphates (ATP, PPi, 1,3-BPG), enol phosphates (PEP), thiol esters (acetyl-CoA), guanidino phosphates (phosphocreatine).
Ranking by −ΔG°′ of hydrolysis: PEP > 1,3-BPG > phosphocreatine > ATP > glucose 6-phosphate, glycerol phosphate; ATP is intermediate.
Compounds above ATP can phosphorylate ADP; ATP phosphorylates those below it.
1,3-BPG + ADP → ATP + 3-phosphoglycerate (substrate-level phosphorylation).
PEP's high potential: hydrolysis gives enol pyruvate, which tautomerizes to stable keto pyruvate (product stabilization).

sections.heading: How ATP does work: group transfer and firefly light
points: ATP usually acts by group transfer, not isolated hydrolysis: phosphoryl transfer → ADP left; pyrophosphoryl → AMP left; adenylyl (AMP) transfer → PPi left.
Hydrolysis-driven conformational cycles power muscle motion and proteins moving along DNA/mRNA (helicases, RecA, topoisomerases, replication ATPases).
Firefly: luciferase uses ATP to activate luciferin → luciferyl adenylate (adenylyl transfer).
With O₂ + luciferase, oxidative decarboxylation → oxyluciferin + light; luciferase structure sets light colour; luciferin regenerated.

mustRemember: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
ΔG°′ = −RT ln K′eq
ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln([products]/[reactants])
Biochemical standard state: pH 7, [H₂O] = 55.5 M, 1 M solutes
ATP hydrolysis ΔG°′ = −30.5 kJ/mol; erythrocyte actual ΔG ≈ −51.82 kJ/mol
Glucose → G6P +13.8 kJ/mol; coupled with ATP → −16.7 kJ/mol
K′eq = 12 → ΔG°′ ≈ −6.15 kJ/mol
1 kcal = 4.184 kJ
Km = [S] at Vmax/2
High-energy compound cutoff: > 7.0 kcal/mol hydrolysis
PEP (enol phosphate), 1,3-BPG (acyl phosphate), phosphocreatine (guanidino phosphate), acetyl-CoA (thiol ester)
MgATP²⁻ is the true enzyme substrate
Firefly: luciferin + ATP → luciferyl adenylate → (O₂) oxyluciferin + light

distinguish.difference: Catabolism: breakdown, energy-releasing, convergent; anabolism: biosynthesis, energy-requiring, divergent.
Exergonic ΔG < 0, releases energy, spontaneous; endergonic ΔG > 0, needs energy input.
ΔG°′ is a fixed constant at standard conditions (from K′eq); ΔG is actual, includes current concentration ratio.
Vmax is maximal rate at saturation; Km is the [S] giving half Vmax.

distinguish.pair: Phosphoryl vs pyrophosphoryl vs adenylyl transfer
distinguish.difference: Leaves ADP, AMP and PPi respectively.

distinguish.pair: ATP → ADP + Pi vs ATP → AMP + PPi
distinguish.difference: Terminal phosphate removal vs pyrophosphate cleavage; both exergonic.
Substrate-level: direct phosphate transfer from an intermediate (1,3-BPG, PEP) to ADP; oxidative: ATP synthesis activated when energy is low.

traps: ΔG°′ is not actual ΔG; only actual ΔG includes concentrations.
Negative ΔG predicts direction, not speed; enzymes change rate, never ΔG.
Km is a substrate concentration, not a rate.
ATP usually works by group transfer (as MgATP²⁻), not by releasing heat from isolated hydrolysis.
ATP is intermediate, not highest, in phosphoryl-transfer potential (PEP, 1,3-BPG, phosphocreatine are higher).
Not all high-energy compounds are phosphates (e.g. acetyl-CoA thioester).

oneLiner: Genetic information flows DNA → RNA → protein via replication, transcription and translation; prokaryotes regulate mainly at transcription initiation, exemplified by the inducible lac operon (repressor + CAP/cAMP) and the repressible trp operon.

sections.heading: Genes and the central dogma
points: Gene = segment of DNA carrying inherited information; contributes to traits and inherited disease.
Central dogma: DNA → RNA → protein (residue-by-residue information flow).
Replication: DNA → DNA; transcription: DNA → RNA; translation: mRNA → protein.
Genes may be constitutive (always on) or inducible (switched on by a signal).

sections.heading: DNA replication
points: Occurs in S phase; semiconservative — each daughter duplex has one parental + one new strand.
Helicase opens DNA at the Y-shaped replication fork.
Leading strand made continuously toward fork movement; lagging strand discontinuously as Okazaki fragments.
RNA primers provide starting points for DNA synthesis.

sections.heading: Transcription and RNA processing
points: RNA polymerase stages: initiation (binds promoter, opens transcription bubble) → promoter escape → elongation → termination.
Location: prokaryotic cytoplasm; eukaryotic nucleus.
Template = antisense/noncoding strand; mRNA is complementary to it.
Coding/sense strand = same sequence as mRNA, with T instead of U.
Eukaryotic pre-mRNA has exons (coding) + introns (noncoding); splicing removes introns and joins exons → mature mRNA.

sections.heading: Translation and protein maturation
points: Occurs on ribosomes in cytoplasm; mRNA = message, tRNA = carries amino acids, ribosome = joins them.
mRNA read 5′ → 3′; protein grows N-terminus → C-terminus.
Protein then folds (chaperones help) and may be transported via ER and Golgi.

sections.heading: Principles of gene regulation
points: Regulation matches gene activity to metabolism, growth, development and differentiation.
Prokaryotes: mainly transcription initiation; no nucleus → transcription and translation simultaneous.
Eukaryotes: regulate transcription, RNA processing, RNA export to cytosol and translation.
Positive regulation ↑ expression (activator/inducer); negative ↓ expression (repressor/inhibitor).
Operon = prokaryotic cluster of related genes under one promoter, transcribed as one mRNA (lac, ara, gal for sugars); not in eukaryotes.

sections.heading: Lac operon: components
points: Lets E. coli use lactose when preferred sugar glucose is unavailable.
lacZ → β-galactosidase (lactose → glucose + galactose; also forms allolactose); lacY → permease (imports lactose); lacA → transacetylase.
Promoter binds RNA polymerase; operator (overlaps promoter) binds lac repressor; CAP site upstream binds CAP.
CAP encoded by a separate gene, made constitutively, but active only when bound to cAMP.

sections.heading: Lac operon: two controls
points: Negative control (lactose arm): no lactose → repressor binds operator, blocks RNA pol; lactose → allolactose binds repressor, releases it.
Inducible operon: default off; allolactose = inducer.
Positive control (glucose arm): low glucose → high cAMP ('hunger signal') → cAMP–CAP binds DNA → helps RNA pol bind → high transcription.
Glucose+/lactose−: none; glucose+/lactose+: low (leaky); glucose−/lactose−: none; glucose−/lactose+: strong.

sections.heading: Trp operon: repressible control
points: Structural genes trpE, trpD, trpC, trpB, trpA on one transcript encode tryptophan-biosynthesis enzymes.
Tryptophan absent: repressor inactive → operon on (default).
Tryptophan present: binds repressor as co-repressor → active complex binds operator → off.
Lac (inducible) and trp (repressible) are both negatively regulated by repressors.

mustRemember: Central dogma: DNA → RNA → protein
Replication: S phase, semiconservative; leading continuous, lagging = Okazaki fragments; RNA primers
Template = antisense; coding strand = mRNA with T for U
Translation: mRNA 5′→3′, protein N→C
lacZ = β-galactosidase, lacY = permease, lacA = transacetylase
Allolactose = lac inducer; tryptophan = trp co-repressor
Low glucose → high cAMP → active CAP → strong transcription
Strong lac transcription only with lactose present AND glucose absent
Glucose + lactose present → low/leaky transcription
Repressor binds operator; RNA pol binds promoter; CAP binds CAP site
Trp genes: trpE, D, C, B, A

distinguish.difference: Template (antisense) is read and is complementary to mRNA; coding (sense) matches mRNA except T vs U.
Leading synthesized continuously toward fork; lagging discontinuously as Okazaki fragments.
Exons coding, retained in mature mRNA; introns noncoding, spliced out.
Repressor: negative control at operator, responds to lactose; CAP: positive control at CAP site, responds to glucose via cAMP.
Lac default off, inducer inactivates repressor; trp default on, co-repressor activates repressor.
Inducer (allolactose) removes repressor from DNA; co-repressor (Trp) enables repressor to bind DNA.
Prokaryotes mainly at transcription initiation with coupled translation; eukaryotes at transcription, processing, export, translation.

traps: Replication/transcription/translation swaps in options: copy DNA / make RNA / make protein.
Template strand = antisense; coding strand resembles mRNA (T vs U).
Lactose alone only removes repression; strong expression also needs low glucose (cAMP–CAP).
CAP is positive, repressor negative — they bind different sites (CAP site vs operator).
Low glucose cannot overcome a bound repressor (glucose−/lactose− = no transcription).
Trp operon is also negatively regulated — 'repressible' does not mean positive control.

oneLiner: Genetic engineering isolates a gene, cuts and ligates it into a vector, transfers it into a host and selects/screens clones; core tools are restriction enzymes, DNA ligase, PCR, gel electrophoresis, Sanger sequencing and CRISPR-Cas9.

sections.heading: Definitions and milestones
points: Genetic engineering = deliberate isolation, modification and transfer of DNA; underlies recombinant DNA technology.
Recombinant DNA = sequences from different sources joined; vector carries it into a host cell.
Clone = genetically identical population from one progenitor cell; transformation = introducing foreign DNA into a host.
Milestones: 1973 first GM bacteria; 1974 GM mice; 1982 commercial insulin-producing bacteria; 1994 GM food sold; 2003 GM pets (GloFish).

sections.heading: Cloning workflow
points: Isolate/PCR-amplify gene → cut insert + vector with compatible restriction enzymes → ligate with DNA ligase → transform host → select & screen → express.
Selection finds cells carrying vector (selectable marker); screening verifies correct recombinant insert.
Construct elements: promoter + terminator (transcription), selectable marker, origin of replication.

sections.heading: Restriction enzymes
points: Restriction endonucleases: bacterial defense enzymes cutting DNA at specific 4–8 bp recognition sites, often palindromic.
Same enzyme on vector and insert → compatible ends.
Sticky (cohesive) ends have single-stranded overhangs that base-pair; blunt ends have none.
Enzyme choice depends on location of recognition sites and needed compatibility.

sections.heading: DNA ligase
points: Seals sugar-phosphate backbone: phosphodiester bond between 3′-OH and 5′-phosphate (seals nicks).
T4 DNA ligase is ATP-dependent: forms ligase–AMP (releasing PPi) → AMP transferred to DNA 5′-phosphate → 3′-OH attacks → bond formed.
Sticky ends ligate more efficiently than blunt (overhang pairing aligns ends, raising effective concentration).

sections.heading: PCR
points: In vitro selective amplification of a DNA region in a thermal cycler; primers define target boundaries.
Components: template DNA, primers, dNTPs, (heat-stable) DNA polymerase, buffer.
Cycle order: denaturation (strand separation by heat) → annealing (primers bind) → extension (polymerase synthesis).
Ideal copies ≈ 2ⁿ after n cycles.
Uses: cloning, pathogen detection, mutation/SNP analysis, sequencing template prep.

sections.heading: Gel electrophoresis and Sanger sequencing
points: DNA's negative phosphate backbone → migrates to positive anode.
Agarose acts as molecular sieve: separation by size; smaller fragments move faster/farther (distance inversely related to size).
Sanger: normal dNTPs + small amount of ddNTPs; ddNTP lacks 3′-OH → chain termination.
Fragments of varying length, each ending at a specific base, reveal sequence.

sections.heading: CRISPR-Cas9
points: Adapted from bacterial antiviral defense; guide RNA gives specificity, Cas9 = nuclease.
gRNA pairs with ~20-nt target adjacent to a PAM; Cas9 makes a double-strand break.
NHEJ: error-prone → indels → gene knockout.
HDR: uses donor DNA template → precise insertion/correction.

sections.heading: Vectors
points: Vector = DNA vehicle carrying foreign DNA into host for replication, sometimes expression.
Needs ori (replication), selectable marker, insertion site (MCS = multiple restriction sites), ability to enter host.
Choice depends on insert size and purpose; expression needs added promoter/expression elements.

mustRemember: PCR copies ≈ 2ⁿ after n cycles
PCR order: denaturation → annealing → extension
Ligase: 3′-OH + 5′-phosphate → phosphodiester bond; T4 ligase uses ATP (ligase–AMP intermediate)
Restriction sites 4–8 bp, often palindromic
DNA migrates to + anode; smaller = farther
ddNTP lacks 3′-OH → chain termination
CRISPR: ~20-nt guide + PAM; Cas9 double-strand break; NHEJ → knockout, HDR → precise edit
Vector essentials: ori, selectable marker, MCS
1973 GM bacteria, 1974 GM mice, 1982 insulin bacteria, 1994 GM food, 2003 GloFish

distinguish.difference: Restriction enzyme cuts at specific sites; ligase joins fragments by phosphodiester bonds.
Sticky have complementary overhangs (more efficient ligation); blunt have none.
Selection retains cells carrying vector (marker); screening identifies clones with desired insert.
dNTP has 3′-OH and extends chain; ddNTP lacks 3′-OH and terminates.
NHEJ error-prone, indels, knockout; HDR template-guided, precise insertion/correction.
PCR amplifies DNA; Sanger reads sequence; CRISPR edits a targeted site.

traps: Restriction enzymes cut, ligase joins — roles often swapped.
Selection ≠ screening.
DNA moves toward the positive electrode; smaller fragments migrate farther (not larger).
Cas9 needs both guide match and an adjacent PAM to cut.
Ligase links 3′-OH to 5′-phosphate (not 5′-OH to 3′-phosphate).

oneLiner: Moving from DNA insert to product: choose cloning vs expression vector, marker/reporter, host and cDNA insert, then run the ordered pipeline (isolate → insert → transform → select → screen → confirm → express → purify) and apply it in medicine, agriculture, industry and environment.

sections.heading: Cloning vectors and plasmids
points: Cloning vector mainly carries/replicates DNA, not necessarily expresses it.
Good plasmid: small, easy to introduce, often high-copy; has ori (sets copy number), selectable marker, MCS.
pBR322: early plasmid with ampicillin- and tetracycline-resistance markers.
pUC: high-copy series used for cloning and blue-white screening.

sections.heading: Expression vectors
points: Contain promoter, translation-initiation signal (RBS) and terminator to make RNA/protein.
pET system: vector in E. coli, IPTG induces T7 promoter → transcription → translation.
IPTG = chemical inducer of lac-controlled expression systems.
A cloning vector is not automatically an expression vector.

sections.heading: Selectable markers vs reporters
points: Selectable marker: survival under selective condition (AmpR → grows on ampicillin; KanR).
Reporter: visible/measurable signal — GFP (fluorescence), lacZ (blue-white screening), luciferase (light).

sections.heading: Host systems
points: E. coli: fast, cheap, high yield, but lacks eukaryotic post-translational modifications (e.g. glycosylation).
Yeast (S. cerevisiae): some PTMs.
Plant cells: scalable but slower.
Mammalian (CHO) cells: most appropriate complex PTMs/quality for therapeutic proteins; slower, costlier.

sections.heading: Recombinant DNA pipeline
points: Isolate gene → insert into vector → transform host → select → screen → confirm → express (induce) → purify.
Transformation: DNA into competent cells; selection: keeps marker-carrying cells; screening: likely recombinants.
Confirmation tests insert directly: colony PCR, restriction digestion or sequencing.
Expression induced only after a correct clone is confirmed.

sections.heading: Gene isolation: genomic DNA vs cDNA
points: Genomic DNA contains introns + regulatory regions.
cDNA made from mature mRNA by reverse transcription → no introns.
Use cDNA to express human/eukaryotic genes in E. coli — bacteria cannot splice introns.
PCR (gene-specific primers) amplifies gene; product purified to remove primers, free nucleotides, enzymes before cloning.

sections.heading: Protein production and purification
points: Induce expression → harvest cells → lyse → bind His-tagged protein to Ni-NTA.
Wash with low imidazole; elute with high imidazole.
Check purity/result by SDS-PAGE.

sections.heading: Applications
points: Four buckets: medicine, agriculture, industry, environment.
Recombinant insulin: expressed and purified from recombinant host.
Hepatitis B vaccine: recombinant HBsAg made in yeast.
Bt crops: express bacterial Cry toxin → insect resistance.
Golden Rice: β-carotene (provitamin A) in endosperm.
Gene therapy: add, replace, silence or edit genetic material.

mustRemember: 8-step pipeline: isolate, insert, transform, select, screen, confirm, express, purify
Vector checklist: ori, selectable marker, MCS (+ promoter, RBS, terminator for expression)
pBR322 = AmpR + TetR; pUC = high-copy, blue-white screening
pET: IPTG induces T7 promoter in E. coli
Markers: AmpR, KanR; reporters: GFP, lacZ, luciferase
cDNA (no introns) for eukaryotic gene expression in bacteria
His-tag → Ni-NTA; low imidazole wash, high imidazole elute; SDS-PAGE check
E. coli lacks PTMs; CHO cells for complex therapeutics
HBV vaccine = HBsAg in yeast; Bt = Cry toxin; Golden Rice = β-carotene in endosperm

distinguish.difference: Cloning vector replicates DNA; expression vector adds promoter, RBS, terminator to produce protein.
Marker confers survival (AmpR); reporter gives detectable signal (GFP, lacZ, luciferase).
Genomic has introns + regulatory DNA; cDNA is reverse-transcribed from mRNA, intron-free.
Selection = carries marker; screening = likely recombinant; confirmation = insert verified by colony PCR/digest/sequencing.
E. coli fast, cheap, no eukaryotic PTMs; mammalian slow, costly, proper complex PTMs.
Bt: insect resistance via Cry toxin; Golden Rice: provitamin A via β-carotene.
Low imidazole washes away contaminants; high imidazole elutes His-tagged protein.

traps: Survival on antibiotic proves marker presence, not the desired insert.
A cloning vector is not automatically an expression vector.
Low imidazole washes, high imidazole elutes — not the reverse.
Don't use genomic DNA to express human genes in E. coli — introns can't be removed.
Bt and Golden Rice solve different problems (insects vs vitamin A deficiency).
